clue.text: Rough man carries blades

indicators.note: to carry something is to hold it within, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: the male pronoun stands for a man
the blades of a boat are its oars, by the flat ends that bite the water

explanation.surface: A tough-looking fellow walks about carrying knives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rough' reads as a description of the man, but it is the definition, as in a rough voice. Blades here belong to a rowing boat, not a knife.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoarse voice sounds harsh and grating, which is the rough quality of a sore throat.

clue.text: Humming birds long ago heading off across border into Peru, finally

indicators.note: when the heading goes, the first letter of the word is removed
to lie across something is to span it, so one piece stretches round the other

parts.note: dodos are birds that died out long ago; lose the first letter

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of each of the words just before it

parts.note: the last letters of these three words

explanation.surface: Hummingbirds and extinct species are being tracked across a frontier into Peru.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Humming birds' looks like the hummingbird, but 'Humming' alone is the definition: in British slang something that hums smells. The dodo is the classic bird of long ago.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang uses humming for giving off a strong smell, a close match for smelly or fragrant.

clue.text: Again join three notes together

parts.note: re is a note of the sol-fa scale
ti is another sol-fa note
E is a note of the musical scale by letter name

explanation.surface: A musician binds three notes into a chord.
explanation.walkthrough: Two notes come from the sol-fa scale (do, re, mi ... ti) and one is a letter name, E.
explanation.definitionFit: To tie something again, fastening a knot a second time, is to rejoin it.

clue.text: Taps into uncomplicated atmosphere that offers comfort

definitions.note: the answer is a noun; the definition describes it as something that offers comfort

indicators.note: going into something means entering it, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: simple, not complicated
taps on a basin are marked C and H, cold and hot
the atmosphere around us is air

explanation.surface: Tapping into a relaxed, simple atmosphere is soothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taps into' sounds like accessing something; the taps are the hot and cold ones, labelled C and H, going into AIR.
explanation.definitionFit: An easy chair is a large upholstered armchair built for relaxing, so its whole purpose is comfort.

clue.text: Want footwear imprinted with right label

indicators.note: something imprinted has marks pressed into it, so letters go inside

parts.note: an item of footwear
R is the standard abbreviation for right
a tag is a label

explanation.surface: Someone longs for shoes stamped with the correct brand label.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Want' reads as a verb of desire but is the noun, as in lack: 'for want of a nail'.
explanation.definitionFit: Want in the old sense of need or lack means not having enough, which is a shortage.

clue.text: Neck down covering for offspring of this?
Bars to close, maybe, in unfashionable, half-demolished thoroughfare

indicators.note: knocking down half of something leaves only half of the word standing

parts.note: what is out is no longer in fashion
a road, of which only the first half survives

explanation.surface: Pubs are closing on a shabby, partly knocked-down street.
explanation.walkthrough: The bars are musical bars, not pubs; 'to close' means to end a piece, and 'maybe' marks this as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: An outro is the closing passage of a song or programme, a set of bars that ends it.

clue.text: Yuck! That is excessively short up top, generating something hard

indicators.note: cutting a word short drops its final letter
in a down answer, what is up top is placed first, at the head of the column

parts.note: too, meaning excessively, with its tail removed
an exclamation of disgust
i.e., the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: Someone recoils at a haircut that is far too short on top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up top' says where the shortened word goes in a down answer: first. 'Short up top' otherwise sounds like a barber's instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A toughie is an informal word for a difficult problem or puzzle, something hard to crack.

clue.text: Come to like Don

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to become keen on a hobby or subject
second meaning: to put on clothes, pulling them on over yourself

explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' looks like a name or a university teacher, but here it is the verb to don, put on clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb covers both developing enthusiasm for an interest and putting on a garment.

clue.text: Aristo abroad has set no clear limits on returning

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the letters read from right to left

indicators.text: has set no clear limits on
indicators.note: with no clear limits, the answer runs across word boundaries inside the words

parts.note: these letters run straight through the words, read backwards

explanation.surface: A foreign aristocrat has laid down no firm rules about coming back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' is part of the hidden string, not a link word; the answer starts in 'clear' and runs back to 'has'.
explanation.definitionFit: A contessa is an Italian countess, a noblewoman found abroad from a British viewpoint.

clue.text: Family member housed in back street digs

indicators.note: to be housed in a place is to live inside it, so one piece goes within another
back means turned round to face the other way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street
an aunt is a relative

explanation.surface: A relative lodges in rented rooms on a back street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'digs' looks like British slang for lodgings, which suits the surface; here it is the plural noun for cutting remarks.
explanation.definitionFit: Digs are sly jibes or pointed remarks, and taunts are insulting jeers of the same kind.

clue.text: Sir Patrick, one hears? Rather, Sir Thomas

indicators.note: what one hears is the sound, not the spelling

parts.note: Sir Patrick Moore was the long-serving British TV astronomer
meaning: to a greater degree, as in 'or less'
meaning: the surname of the Tudor statesman who wrote Utopia

explanation.surface: A quiz asks which famous knight is meant: Patrick, or rather Thomas.
explanation.walkthrough: Patrick Moore presented The Sky at Night on British TV for decades; his surname sounds the same as the Tudor saint's.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an adverb of degree like rather, and the surname of Henry VIII's executed chancellor.

clue.text: Suspicious phone call about drug packaging, that's clear

indicators.note: something suspicious is not straight, so these letters are crooked and out of order

parts.note: taken as written
E is ecstasy

explanation.surface: A dodgy phone call about a drug shipment, and the police say the case is clear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'packaging, that's clear' reads like two remarks, but together they describe the transparent wrapping.
explanation.definitionFit: Cellophane is a thin transparent film used to wrap goods, see-through packaging material.

clue.text: Sickly Martha's lacking resistance to condition

indicators.note: something sickly is out of sorts, so the letters are in poor order
to lack something is to be without it, so a letter is taken out

parts.note: taken as written, with the S of the possessive
R is the symbol for electrical resistance; it is removed

explanation.surface: Frail Martha has no resistance to some illness.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suits the answer: a sickly person with low resistance may well suffer from a breathing complaint.
explanation.definitionFit: Asthma is a chronic medical complaint of the airways, a long-term illness or disorder.

clue.text: Cat's backside cleared of parasite

indicators.note: cleared of something means rid of it, so those letters are removed

parts.note: the rear end
a bot is a parasitic fly larva; these letters go

explanation.surface: A vet removes a parasite from a cat's rear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cat's' is Cat is: the definition plus a link. The bot fly larva is a parasite of horses and sheep.
explanation.definitionFit: A tom is a male domestic cat, one specific kind of the animal.

clue.text: Blazing with the oxygen injected at extreme temperature

indicators.note: a blazing thing is wild and fierce, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen
surface padding: it only says the gas is added to the mix

explanation.surface: A furnace roars when oxygen is pumped in to reach fierce heat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blazing' looks like the definition, sitting at the start, but it only stirs up the letters; the definition is at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Metal heated beyond red glows white, so white-hot describes being heated to an extreme degree.

clue.text: One investigating report of local ghost?

indicators.note: a report is something said and heard, so the sound counts, not the spelling

parts.note: local gives IN (at home, as in the local pub being the one you are in) and a ghost is a spectre

explanation.surface: Someone looks into accounts of a haunting in the neighbourhood.
explanation.walkthrough: The ghost-hunting surface makes 'One investigating' look like a paranormal researcher; it is the police rank.
explanation.definitionFit: An inspector is a police officer or official whose job is examining and looking into cases.

clue.text: Grant possibly rumoured to be cut

indicators.note: a rumour is passed on by word of mouth, so the sound is what matters

parts.note: Hugh Grant is the film actor, one possible Grant

explanation.surface: A grant of funding is rumoured to be facing the axe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grant' reads as money; 'possibly' says it is an example, here the actor Hugh Grant.
explanation.definitionFit: To hew is to chop or hack at wood or stone with an axe, a way of cutting.

clue.text: Rejection of novel by unknown ultimately unfair, journalist complained

indicators.note: to reject is to throw back, so these letters are turned round

parts.note: Emma is Jane Austen's novel
y is an algebraic unknown

indicators.note: ultimately means at the very end, so only the final letter counts

parts.note: the last letter of the word
ed is short for editor

explanation.surface: A writer grumbled that a publisher's turning down a novel by an unknown author was unfair.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversal takes the novel and the unknown together: EMMA followed by Y, all turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: To yammer is to whine or grumble at length, an informal word for moaning and complaining.

clue.text: Fantastic, but dated, hotel encapsulates old classical city

indicators.note: to encapsulate is to enclose in a capsule, so one piece is held inside

parts.note: antic is an old adjective for grotesque or bizarre
O is the abbreviation for old
H is hotel in the phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A grand, faded hotel sits in the middle of an ancient city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'but dated' flags that the word for fantastic is archaic. ANTIC and H together surround O.
explanation.definitionFit: Antioch was a major city of the Hellenistic and Roman world, in modern Turkey.

clue.text: Demo slashed by 40%, overlooked by county, concerning local bigwig

indicators.note: cutting forty per cent of a five-letter word removes two of its letters
in a down answer, what overlooks sits above, so it comes first

parts.note: Mayo is a county in the west of Ireland
a rally is a demonstration; lose the last two of its five letters

explanation.surface: A protest is cut back, with the county council watching, over some local dignitary.
explanation.walkthrough: The Irish county sits on top of the cut-down rally in this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Mayoral is the adjective relating to a mayor, the civic head who is a town's leading figure.

clue.text: Absorbing times doing what results in …?

indicators.note: to absorb is to soak up and take in, so one piece swallows another

parts.note: taken as written
T is time, so two of them for the plural

explanation.surface: A clue about engrossing times, trailing off into an ellipsis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doing' is both wordplay and part of the definition; the three dots in the clue are the result of the activity described.
explanation.definitionFit: Marking a row of points on paper produces an ellipsis, the three-point punctuation shown in the clue.

clue.text: Toboggan, impeded by damp, losing rear end, spun awkwardly

indicators.note: losing the rear end means the last letter falls away
something impeded has an obstacle stuck in its path, so a piece is lodged inside

parts.note: a sled is a toboggan
wet, with its final letter lost

explanation.surface: A sledge slowed by wet snow loses its back end and skids sideways.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a tobogganing mishap; the wordplay holds a clipped word for damp inside SLED.
explanation.definitionFit: To slew is to swing or skid round sideways out of control, so slewed means turned clumsily.

clue.text: Horsewoman always accepts direction given by conservationists

indicators.note: to accept is to take in, so one piece is received inside another

parts.note: ever means always, as in ever hopeful
E is east, a compass direction
the National Trust, the British heritage and conservation charity, abbreviated NT

explanation.surface: A rider always takes guidance from the conservation groups.
explanation.walkthrough: The National Trust is a British charity that looks after historic houses and countryside; its initials follow the compass point inside EVER.
explanation.definitionFit: An eventer competes in eventing, the equestrian sport of dressage, cross-country and jumping, so is one kind of rider.

clue.text: Yes, sir, Cath's misbehaving with tongue, sticking it out

indicators.note: misbehaving means acting out of line, so the letters leave their proper order

parts.note: taken as written; the 's that follows is is
taken as written

explanation.surface: Cath says 'yes, sir' while cheekily poking her tongue out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sticking it out' fits the tongue in the surface picture, but it is the definition: persevering. Cath's is Cath is.
explanation.definitionFit: Staying the course, from racing, means persevering to the finish without giving up, enduring.

clue.text: Dave blowing top in tight spots

definitions.note: the naevi are spots; 'tight' fills out the familiar phrase for surface

indicators.note: the top of a down word is its first letter, which goes
blowing things scatters them about, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: the name without its first letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: Dave loses his temper when he is in a difficult position.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blowing top' reads as losing your temper; it is two signals: scramble, and lose the top letter. 'in' is fodder, not a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Naevi are birthmarks or moles, small coloured marks on the skin, plural of naevus.

clue.text: Drove ball, umpire's call abruptly being reversed

indicators.note: abruptly means cut off suddenly, so the word stops before its last letter
reversed means turned back to front, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: deuce, the tennis umpire's call at forty all, missing its final letter

explanation.surface: A tennis player hit the ball hard after the umpire's call was overturned.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is tennis, but the answer belongs to snooker and billiards, where the ball is struck with a cue.
explanation.definitionFit: To cue is to strike a billiard or snooker ball with the long tapered stick, so cued means hit it.

clue.text: Cost nearly something astronomical

indicators.note: nearly means not quite complete, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: come to, as in the bill came to twenty pounds

explanation.surface: The price was almost sky-high.
explanation.walkthrough: 'astronomical' suggests an enormous price, but it is literal: a body in space.
explanation.definitionFit: A comet is an icy body orbiting the Sun with a glowing tail, an object studied in astronomy.

clue.text: See 24
Friendly hint

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an adjective, close and familiar
second meaning: a verb, to suggest indirectly

explanation.walkthrough: The two senses are pronounced differently: the adjective ends like 'mit', the verb like 'mate'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both an adjective for close personal familiarity and a verb for suggesting something without stating it.

clue.text: Henry and Brunel will stop Carol and Bob once

indicators.note: a stopper plugs a gap, so these letters fill the middle of the other word

parts.note: to carol is to sing
H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance
Brunel is this puzzle's setter, so Brunel will is I will, shortened

explanation.surface: Henry and the engineer Brunel will halt Carol and Bob.
explanation.walkthrough: Brunel is the setter's pseudonym, so the setter's 'will' is I'll. Bob was slang for a shilling, a coin in British money before 1971.
explanation.definitionFit: Bob is old British slang for a shilling, the coin worth twelve pence before decimalisation.

clue.text: Comeback by Red Queen, a cutting remark

indicators.note: a comeback is a return trip, so the letters go back the way they came

parts.note: a Trot is a Trotskyist, a left-winger
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: The Red Queen fires back with a sharp remark, as in Lewis Carroll.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comeback' looks like the definition, since a retort is a comeback; it only turns the pieces round. The definition is at the far end.
explanation.definitionFit: A retort is a sharp, witty reply made in answer to another remark, often biting in tone.
